title: A Door Left Open, A Life Cut Short
author: Nainika Shivaram
excerpt: A fatal dispute aboard a Mumbai local train has reignited concerns over passenger safety and the legal consequences of public violence.
content:
Date | Location:
July 2 | Mumbai

Lead:
A routine commute on a Mumbai local train turned tragic when 22 year old Mayank Lohar was fatally stabbed after an argument over whether the compartment door should remain open during heavy rainfall.

Background:
The incident occurred aboard the Churchgate–Nallasopara fast local in the first class compartment between Andheri and Borivali stations. According to investigators, an argument over closing the train door escalated into violence, resulting in the fatal stabbing of Mayank Lohar.

Key Developments:
Police alleged that the accused, Roshan Suvarna, 30, of Mira Bhayandar, stabbed Lohar multiple times before fleeing the train near Borivali. Following an approximately 15 hour manhunt, the Government Railway Police arrested him in Panvel. As of the July 2 dateline, the accused was in police custody while investigators continued collecting evidence and examining the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Legal Significance:
The case has renewed concerns about passenger safety on Mumbai's suburban railway network and highlights the severe legal consequences of violent offences committed in public spaces. Investigators are also examining whether the attack arose spontaneously or whether the accused's possession of a knife before the incident has any bearing on the nature of the offence.

Next Steps:
The investigation is ongoing, with police expected to complete further forensic and witness examinations before filing a chargesheet. The matter will proceed through the criminal justice process, where the evidence gathered during the investigation will determine the charges and subsequent court proceedings.

title: Mental Health and Human Rights in Educational institutions.
author: Nishalya Singh
excerpt: Is student mental health a welfare measure or a legal right? This article explores the duty of educational institutions to safeguard mental well-being.
content:
Universities and Higher Educational institutions across the globe are designed to be institutions responsible for the developing the growing mind of a student, students which would later form the vanguard for the future of the world. To become leaders in their respective fields, students go through a diverse and challenging curriculum, one that involves immense dedication and perseverance. To overcome the challenges posed during this crucial chapter of their lives, it is essential for a student to keep a check on their Mental Health. For the longest time, educational institutions have treated student mental health as a matter of discretionary welfare, it is designed merely as a “nice to have” voluntary obligation rather than a core one. This framework needs to be challenged. The idea of mental health deserving the same protection as physical health is not a new concept, it has been debated and discussed across various sectors throughout the world. Academicians across the world argue that mental well-being is not simply a service that institutions may choose to provide or adhere, but a right that every student is entitled to, grounded in principles of International human rights law, domestic legislation and long-standing principles of institutional duty of care.

The Legal Foundations deriving Mental Health as a Right

The World Health Organization’s 1948 constitution famously defined health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease. This definition has since been absorbed into international instruments. Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights recognizes an individual’s right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and his family, while Article 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights goes further, guaranteeing the right to the “highest attainable standard of Physical and Mental Health.” These Articles and Subsequent interpretative guidance from the UN treaty bodies have made it clear that these practices enable and obligates states and by extension, public institutions actively funded and regulated by the state to address mental health concerns faced by an individual rather than remain passive.

The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) extends this logic to psychological disabilities, enabling the requirement of providing dedicated accommodations in educational institutions to not segregate students which are disadvantaged because of their mental health concerns. These instruments at large frame mental well-being as inseparable from human dignity. An individual’s capacity for autonomous decision making, social participation and development of the self is compromised if the individual concerned suffers from mental health issues which lead to psychological instability, denying the right to provide assistance or help to the concerned individuals particularly wherever an institution has the power and resources to prevent harm. This ends up becoming a violation of the rights of an individual rather than a private tragedy.

Institutional Duty of Care

Alongside International human rights frameworks, common law systems across the world have developed their own mechanism for holding institutions accountable for mental health rights violations, the doctrine of the Duty of Care. Historically rooted in the concept of in loco parentis the doctrine’s underlying logic is that institutions that exercise significant control over an individual’s daily environment and can reasonably foresee risks within that environment, the institution bears some responsibility for mitigating those risks owing to established relationships of control, dependence and vulnerability.

To bring the mental health of a student in context, this means that when an educational institution is aware or should be reasonably aware of a student’s psychological distress and fails to address those concerns proportionately, it can be exposed to liability under principles of negligence. Courts in several jurisdictions have grappled with cases involving student suicides or mishandled disclosures, examining whether institutions ignored warning signs exhibited by a student or breached confidentiality in ways that compounded harm rather than alleviated it. A recent judgement is that of the Delhi High Court in W.P. (CRL) 793/2017 in RE: Suicide committed by Sushant Rohilla, Law student of I.P. University, wherein the student owing to the inability to meet the mandated attendance requirements of the university was barred from giving the end term examinations and repeat a year, which forced the student to take such an extreme step. Other similar incidents have also been considered by the Supreme Court in two recent decisions, i.e Amit Kumar & Ors. Union of India & Ors., 2025 INSC 385 and Sukdeb Saha v. The State of Andhra Pradesh & Ors., 2025 INSC 893. In the case of Amit Kumar & Ors v. Union of India, two students of IIT Delhi were found dead under suspicious circumstances in their hostels wherein the family members had sought registration of an FIR. The police concluded under Section 174 of Cr.P.C. that the said students had committed suicide owing to depression as they could not cope with their studies. The court issued a direction to undertake a re-evaluation of the mandatory attendance norms and directed the BCI to “incorporate modification of attendance norms,” “contemplate flexibility in attendance requirements” and consider “ameliorative measures.” While this directive proved helpful to the students, institutions countrywide disagreed with this directive issued by the Delhi HC and multiple petitions were filed to reinforce attendance norms, which led to the intervention of the Supreme Court which Stayed the order passed by the Delhi HC. Thus, these cases grapple with a critical legal question which increasingly shapes institutional policy, not simply whether a tragedy occurred but whether it was foreseeable and preventable.

Policy Frameworks: Progress on Paper, Gaps in Practice

In many countries, legislative and policy frameworks have begun to catch up with Rights based approaches even If their implementation lags. For example, the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 in India marked a significant shift towards a rights-based model, decriminalizing suicide attempts and affirming a person’s right to access mental healthcare with dignity. University Grants Commission guidelines direct higher educational institutions to establish counselling centres and to train faculty members as informal counsellors, while the National Education Policy 2020 speaks to a more “holistic” approach to student development, including flexible assessments and ensuring reduced academic stress.

These frameworks however often remain aspirational. Mental Health legislation is rarely written with educational campuses in mind, leaving a regulatory gap. Guidelines calling for counselling centres frequently lack enforcement mechanisms, and certain institutions merely keep these centres on paper to avoid institutional penalties. Structural shortcomings compound this issue, many countries including India, face a severe scarcity of Mental Health professionals relative to the population size, highlighting the lack of adequate staff to meet the institutional demand.

Another persistent ethical issue is Stigma. When Mental health struggles are treated as personal weakness rather than a systematic issue requiring an institutional response, students particularly those from marginalized or first-generation backgrounds are further discouraged from accessing available support. The silence to address concerns obscures the true scale of need for mental health obligations, making it easier for institutions and policymakers to under-invest in these core services.

CONCLUSION

The conversation around student mental health has shifted meaningfully over the past decade, from a private, individualized issue to one increasingly recognized as a matter of institutional and legal responsibility. International human rights instruments, evolving doctrines of negligence and duty of care and domestic legislation all point in the same direction, educational institutions are not merely educators but also act as custodians of the student. Laws and guidelines while existent in most jurisdictions lack enforcement. Institutional cultures often treat mental health crisis as an unfortunate exception rather than a foreseeable and preventable failure. Closing this gap will take more than the passing of another policy document, it requires binding standards with entailed consequences for non-compliance, sustained investment in trained staff and the initiative to begin a cultural shift within institutions to address mental health concerns and ensure prevention of harm rather than responding after the damage is done. Making good on the right to mental well-being in higher educational institutions is not a matter of charity or goodwill; it is a matter of dignity, equity and the basic promise every institution makes to the student it admits.

SOURCES:

title: Juvenile Justice: Rehabilitation versus punishment.
author: Nainika Shivaram
excerpt: Should juvenile justice prioritize rehabilitation or punishment? This opinion explores the need for accountability while preserving opportunities for reform.
content:
The issue of a juvenile's involvement in a serious crime is always present. If a child commits a crime should he/she be treated like an adult or should the law be concerned with rehabilitation? When public outrage is there, they want more severe punishment, particularly if the crime is severe. It's not difficult to see why. It's time for justice for the victims and accountability for those who should be held responsible. However, justice is not just about punishment. It's also a matter of determining whether a young wrongdoer can change.

I think the juvenile justice system should continue to place emphasis on rehabilitation instead of punishment, but not to the detriment of punishment. The opportunity to change should be provided for all children, but at no expense to public safety or the rights of the innocent victim.

Children think, make decisions and react to their environment in different ways to adults.[1] Juvenile offenders who enter into the juvenile justice system often have challenging backgrounds that involve poverty, abuse, neglect, familial substance abuse, and/or lack of education.[2] None of these factors gives an excuse to commit crimes, but they help to explain why some children are driven to commit crime.

Rehabilitation is not about forgiveness of crime, or the wiping away of consequences. The aim is to minimize the risk of this child reoffending. Counselling, Education, Vocational Training, Psychological Support, and Family Intervention can aid a young offender to put their life back together.[3] In that respect, rehab is for everybody.

But rehabilitation cannot be the blanket solution for all juvenile delinquents. Some crimes are so senseless and violent that they bring up significant questions of maturity and understanding of the perpetrators. The Nirbhaya case of 2012 in Delhi, where a girl was raped in the national capital, put a new slant on the discussion of juvenile justice in India.[4] The anger sparked significant judicial changes such as the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act amendment 2015, which provides for a prelim assessment of children aged between 16 and 18 years accused of heinous offences before deciding to try them as adults.[5]

This seems a fairly good middle ground to me. It does not presume that all juveniles are automatically presumed to be grown-ups, nor does it presume that all children cannot understand the gravity of their behavior. Rather, it enables the courts to take into account the mental state, maturity, and context of the crime before deciding that. Age shouldn't be the sole criterion for giving justice. It should also take into account purpose, comprehension and the potential for change.

Meanwhile, rehabilitation must be more meaningful than putting a kid in an observation home. The infrastructure, the number of trained counsellors, overcrowding in juvenile homes and poor monitoring are some of the issues that cause lack of infrastructure.[6] In the case of rehabilitation, the system has to provide quality education, mental health care, skill development, and good reintegration into society. If these measures are not implemented, rehabilitation would only be a promise on paper.

Victim voices should continue to be at the heart of the justice system. The rehabilitation process must not mask the suffering of victims and their families.[7] Compassion for the victim and the child offender must be present in a spirit of justice, but compassion should never be used to excuse a child's responsibility. If a juvenile commits a serious crime, he or she is responsible and will learn the consequences.

A choice between rehabilitation and punishment is not an either/or scenario. A just juvenile justice system should be one that is both accountable and offers opportunity for change. Children can do terrible things, but so many can do amazing things if they are provided with the right guidance and support. That should never be forgotten by society. It has to remain fair, weighing and receptive to victims' interests at the same time, while ensuring the maintenance of the rule of law. After all, the real power of a justice system does not just rest on the power to punish evil, but also the power to change lives for the better while advancing the safety of the community.

title:
THE CATCH-22 OF JOHN AND JANE DOES:
Costs and Benefits of the Right to Digital Anonymity
author: Kristalline Hadjirul
excerpt: Can digital anonymity protect free speech without enabling cybercrime? This article explores the legal challenge of balancing privacy with public safety.
content:
“He alone, who owns the Youth, gains the future.”
On the surface, this adage provides wisdom on the importance of youth and their role in nation-building. The maxim appears well-meaning until discovered that the person who uttered these words is none other than Adolf Hitler.[1]

Now that it is known that Adolf Hitler said these words, the statement immediately becomes alarming, especially after realizing that the Nazi regime used to indoctrinate the youth with their racial beliefs. Nobody who knows history wants to quote a tyrant like Adolf Hitler. Nevertheless, what Hitler said about the youth is not per se wrong because the youth is indeed the leaders of tomorrow, and if one seeks to maintain power in the future, they must also secure the youth.

This little exercise demonstrates that there is power and credibility among statements uttered in anonymity. An idea can be powerful if expressed anonymously, but it can also be dangerous if stated anonymously. Identity puts matters into context and can shatter the credibility of anonymous claims. However, in today’s digital age, is it even possible to police the John and Jane Does of the World Wide Web? This article examines and evaluates how different jurisdictions have attempted to balance the right to digital anonymity against the growing need for cybersecurity and public safety.

Anonymity as a Human Right

Since time immemorial, anonymity has facilitated the freedom to express oneself and is especially important in countries where freedom of expression is heavily censored.[2] In the 1780s, American founding fathers Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay used the collective pseudonym Publius to publish the Federalist Papers in advocating for the ratification of the United States Constitution.[3] These publications changed the course of history and proved the powerful impact of the exercise of freedom of expression coupled with anonymity. It is a testament that anonymity can strengthen discourse.

Avowedly, the right to anonymity is not as explicitly recognized as a human right compared to the right to privacy[4] and the right to freedom of expression[5] which serve as its pillars and foundations. Nonetheless, the right to anonymity is a derivative human right that is vital to the exercise of privacy and freedom of expression, and these freedoms are not something that people can easily give up. Indeed, how can persons truly, freely, and uninhibitedly express themselves if statements can be traced back to them with fear of repercussion?

Unfortunately, at present, anonymity is no longer just a facility for freedom of expression but is also a factory of deception and fake news after the dawn of digitalization and artificial intelligence. While anonymity can protect people from censorship and retaliation, it can also protect deception and evasion of liability. Thus, the question now is where to draw the line between anonymity as a human right and anonymity as a security threat?

Anonymity as a Security Threat

The World Wide Web is an enormous space that is vast enough to facilitate global communication and exchange information.[6] In this digital space, everybody is generally free and equal because of the built-in anonymity provided by the platform. There is little to no police, and there are limited legal and institutional safeguards.[7] These terms make the internet a haven for criminals in the following ways, among others:

a.     Anonymization networks and artificial intelligence allow criminals to conceal their identity to evade liability. Criminals can hide their identity by posing as fake persons, impersonating somebody, or appearing completely anonymous and untraceable through the use of artificial intelligence, anonymization networks like Tor, virtual private networks, and other available tools to conceal identifiers like IP addresses and geographical location.
b.     Cryptocurrency and decentralized financial institutions permit criminals to facilitate ransomware payments with little detection. Criminals can use cryptocurrencies and other new forms of digital currency that are unregulated by a state’s central bank to launder money originating from unlawful activities. Being unregulated, the state has limited detection and control over such transactions.
c.      Advances in artificial intelligence and cybertechnology enables criminals to concoct newer forms of phishing and scamming schemes. Criminals are now upgrading their scamming capabilities by capitalizing on the advent of artificial intelligence and newer forms of cybertechnology like voice cloning, deepfake, and others, to support their illicit activities. Non-tech-savvy people are more at risk of becoming victims to these novel schemes.

To make matters worse, digital anonymity is also evolving into a state-destabilizing tool for promoting misinformation and disinformation in order to divide a nation.[8] Such is especially dangerous because nefarious individuals can manipulate public opinion for their own interests and erode public trust while completely evading any liability. This is creating a difficult tension between the need to protect a person’s right to freedom of expression and digital anonymity versus the right against security threats.

Finding the Balance

Admittedly, for many states, the World Wide Web remained as is for many years, ungoverned and unpoliced. However, as cybercrimes have become increasingly prevalent, states have no choice but to find ways to strike a balance in protecting the right to digital anonymity and safeguarding against the security threats digital anonymity is creating.

The United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (“UNESCO”) proposed guidelines in finding the said balance.[9] UNESCO suggested that states should govern and regulate digital platforms by coordinating with the relevant stakeholders to ensure that platforms adhere to international human rights standards but remain transparent to enable freedom of expression.[10] This suggestion is admirable, but it appears general as it operates under the presumption that criminal activities happen only within known digital platforms, when cybercrimes and artificial intelligence-enabled crimes are multi-faceted and cross over both the digital and physical world. Nonetheless, such proposal is a laudable effort to find the balance.

In finding the balance, the members of the European Union promulgated the General Data Protection Regulation[11] which establishes a comprehensive framework for the lawful processing of personal data. This regulation recognizes the right to digital anonymity by requiring personal data to be processed according to the specified standards yet draws a different line when a crime is committed. Where disclosure is required by law, controllers and processors may disclose personal data to competent authorities to facilitate the prevention, investigation, detection, or prosecution of criminal offenses. This regulation really sought to strike a balance between protecting the right to anonymity and heavily restricting data extraction but ended up creating a very complex framework which may be difficult to implement.

In Asia, the People’s Republic of China approached the dilemma differently, by weighing the scale and finding for itself that digital anonymity as a security threat is a heavier issue than digital anonymity as a human right. It thus promulgated its controversial Internet Identification System by allowing citizens to apply for a national virtual identification using their identification cards and facial recognition to curtail security threats nurtured by online anonymity.[12] This decision drew criticisms, but Chinese authorities justify the same as necessary to combat fraud, misinformation, and cybercrimes.

Overall, the gavel falls on states to weigh the costs and benefits of digital anonymity when applied in their territory and find the correct balance between the right to digital anonymity and the threat of digital anonymity because if left unchecked and unbalanced, emerging cyber and artificial intelligence-enabled crimes may pose unprecedented threats to individuals, institutions, and democratic societies. Just as the opening statement demonstrates, ideas may gain credibility when divorced from identity. In the worst case, no one can be sure what to believe anymore, because no one is liable.

title: Copyright Laws and AI: The Delhi High Court’s Stance
author: Sanskrati Jain
excerpt: A look at the Delhi High Court's landmark interim ruling on AI training, fair dealing, and the future of copyright law in India.
content:
Lead: Based on the Delhi High Court’s recent interim judgement,[1] AI platforms storing information to train large language models (LLMs) is not an infringement of Indian copyright laws.

Background: The Asian News International (ANI) and other publications including the Digital News Publishers Association, the association of almost every major media house such as The Times Group, Hindustan, The Hind and India Today Group, filed a suit in 2024 , claiming that OpenAI was using their content without permission to train and operate ChatGPT.[2] However, OpenAI argued that no entity holds a monopoly on facts, adding that news organisations preferring not to have their content scraped can easily block the company’s web crawler.

Key Developments: The Court ruled that training ChatGPT on ANI's content qualifies as fair dealing under Section 52(1)(a)[3], so it doesn't infringe copyright under Section 51[4]. It also found ChatGPT's outputs were not substantially similar to ANI's content, with no proof of memorisation or regurgitation. Since ANI failed to show a prima facie case and the balance of convenience favoured OpenAI, the Court denied the interim injunction — citing potential harm to public interest as well.

Legal Significance: This is one of India's first rulings on AI training and copyright, offering early guidance where legislation is still lacking. By applying fair dealing to LLM training under Section 52(1)(a), the Court distinguished training from outputs — noting infringement could still arise from substantial similarity or memorisation, which ANI failed to prove. Though only an interim order, it's likely to become an influential reference point as AI-copyright litigation evolves.

BIBLIOGRAPHY

1.     ANI Media (P) Ltd. v. OpenAI OpCo LLC, CS(COMM) 1028/2024 (Del. H.C. July 24, 2026) (India). One outlet (thelegalwire.ai) reports a neutral citation of 2026 DHC 5900; this has not been independently corroborated against the judgment cover page or a cause list, so it is omitted from the primary citation pending confirmation.
2.     The Copyright Act, 1957, § 52(1)(a).
3.     The Copyright Act, 1957, § 51.

title: Self-Defense or Aggression? The Hollow Legal Justification for Striking Iran.
author: Nwanguma Rosemary Chinonso
excerpt: An opinion on the legality of U.S. military actions against sovereign states, examining the principles of sovereignty, self-defence, and the United Nations Charter.
content:
The United States is a key player in the international economy, wielding immense political, military, and economic power. In my view, the greatest danger of such unparalleled influence lies in the ease with which it can be exercised against sovereign nations to bend them to its whims and caprices. If a state with such global dominance chooses to attack another sovereign nation, what then becomes of the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity upon which modern international law is founded?

It is my considered opinion that recent precedents under President Donald Trump reveal a disturbing pattern of aggression. To me, they portray the United States less as a defender of the rules-based international order and more as a self-appointed global watchdog that increasingly acts as judge, jury, and, at times, executioner in international affairs.

Article 2(4) of the United Nations Charter expressly prohibits “the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.” Against this legal backdrop, it is necessary to examine instances where, in my opinion, the United States has acted in a manner inconsistent with these foundational principles and, by extension, against the sovereignty of other states.

Let me cast your mind back to 3 January 2026, when Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was arrested on charges of Narco-Terrorism Conspiracy, Cocaine Importation Conspiracy, Possession of Machine Guns and Destructive Devices, and Conspiracy to Possess Machine Guns and Destructive Devices. He was reportedly captured through ‘Operation Absolute Resolve’ and brought from Venezuela, a sovereign nation of over 28 million people to stand trial in Manhattan.

In my view, this action raises profound legal questions under Article 2(1) and Article 2(3) of the United Nations Charter, which affirm the sovereign equality of all member states and require international disputes to be settled through peaceful means in such a manner that international peace and justice are not endangered. To me, this operation reflects a troubling disregard for the sovereign equality that the Charter seeks to guarantee.

How can a state truly be regarded as sovereign if its political leader can be captured and removed to another jurisdiction to face the justice of another nation? In my opinion, this strikes at the very heart of sovereignty. It also raises a legitimate question: how can the international community be entirely certain that such charges are free from political influence or geopolitical interests? These are questions that deserve serious consideration rather than outright dismissal.

In my view, the United States’ approach also raises difficult questions concerning the limits of international jurisdiction. While Article 27 of the Rome Statute removes immunity for heads of state accused of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court, I contend that relying upon such principles outside the framework established by international law risks creating the perception that powerful states may unilaterally determine when and how justice should be enforced. To me, this represents an affront to the sovereignty guaranteed under the United Nations Charter.

Supporting this concern, Margaret Satterthwaite, the United Nations Special Rapporteur, observed in an interview with Al Jazeera that “there is a very clear limit of enforcement jurisdiction internationally; a state cannot enforce its laws on another territory without the consent of that state.” In my opinion, this statement captures one of the central legal concerns surrounding the expanding reach of unilateral enforcement actions. It also reflects the views of many international legal commentators who question the legality of such operations.

Now consider Iran’s current conflict, which emerged from the long-standing dispute surrounding its nuclear programme and escalated following the assassination of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on 28 February 2026. The conflict has since developed into a full-scale war involving both the United States and Israel. In my opinion, what began as a geopolitical dispute has evolved into a humanitarian tragedy marked by continuous retaliation and devastating loss of life.

To me, this conflict further illustrates the consequences of the United States increasingly assuming the role of the world’s self-appointed watchdog. A nation that continues to grapple with serious domestic challenges should, in my view, exercise far greater restraint before positioning itself as the global enforcer of international order.

Another instance that, in my opinion, reflects this pattern of aggression is the United States-led campaign in the Red Sea, where coalition forces have repeatedly launched airstrikes and naval bombardments against Houthi infrastructure in Yemen, citing the protection of international commercial shipping as justification. While safeguarding maritime trade is undoubtedly important, I contend that such operations continue to raise legitimate concerns regarding proportionality, necessity, and respect for the sovereignty of the affected state. To me, this is yet another example of the United States positioning itself as the principal arbiter of international affairs, often at the expense of another state’s sovereignty.

The lessons of history should not be ignored. The Nuremberg Trials of 1946 established one of the most important precedents in international criminal law by affirming that state officials could be held individually accountable for acts of aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. The trials followed the Holocaust, during which approximately six million Jews and millions of others, including Roma, persons with disabilities, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war, Jehovah’s Witnesses, and political dissidents were systematically murdered. In my view, the enduring legacy of Nuremberg is that no nation, regardless of its power or influence, should consider itself above the law.

Another example is Syria, whose government has repeatedly condemned United States military operations as “reckless and irresponsible.” Although the United States has justified many of these actions on security grounds, I believe they continue to generate serious legal controversy. This differs from counterterrorism operations in Somalia, where military actions have often been undertaken in cooperation with the Somali government against Al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia.

Finally, it is my opinion that the Syrian conflict also demonstrates how geopolitical influence can reshape the foreign policy of weaker states. I believe President Ahmed al-Sharaa has chosen political alignment with the United States rather than openly challenging its actions. Whether one agrees with that assessment or not, it reinforces my broader concern that states unwilling to align with U.S. interests often face military intervention, diplomatic isolation, or severe economic pressure, as Cuba has experienced through decades of sanctions and other restrictive measures.

Ultimately, I contend that international law cannot remain credible if its principles are applied selectively. Sovereignty cannot become a privilege reserved for powerful states while weaker nations are expected to comply unconditionally with the rules of the international legal order. If the United Nations Charter is to retain its authority, then its protections must apply equally to every state, irrespective of its military strength, political influence, or economic dominance.

title: Prosecution of Deepfake Crimes: How Indian Courts Are Building a Doctrine without a Statute
author: Anjaneya Pai
excerpt: Prosecution of Deepfake Crimes: How Indian Courts Are Building a Doctrine without a Statute
content:
"We may take judicial notice of the fact that we are living in the era of deepfakes” was the acknowledgement of the Delhi High Court in the case of Nirmaan Malhotra v. Tushita Kaul[1], wherein a husband presented images alleging his wife’s adultery to the Court, in the course of challenging a maintenance order passed by the Court.

It has been observed that such issues have confronted Indian Courts since 2023, as evidenced by Anil Kapoor v. Simply Life India & Ors., wherein the Delhi High Court granted an injunction restraining sixteen entities and, notably, the world at large, from utilising the veteran Bollywood actor's name, likeness, image, or AI/face-morphing/GIF tools for commercial or financial gain without obtaining his consent. This case — the foremost judgment adjudicating an AI-generated deepfake — is said to reflect a disparity in accessibility to litigation: content of a commercial nature is more easily taken down than sexualised deepfake content, as observed by Tech Law Forum, run by the students of NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad[2].

Deepfake crime may be said to range across identity theft, financial fraud, electoral disinformation, non-consensual intimate imagery, and defamation, each testing statutes that remain unequipped to adjudicate such conduct, since existing legislation was not designed to assess AI-generated harm. With a layering of old criminal provisions, freshly notified intermediary rules, and a judiciary willing to stretch constitutional doctrine to fill gaps that Parliament has been slower to close, deepfake crimes in India are adjudicated.

In Light of the Statute

Section 66[3] of the Information Technology Act[4] is broad enough to accommodate penalization of certain dimensions of cyber related offences; it may be understood as the handle of an umbrella with distinct canopies,

1.         Section 66A[5] penalises offensive messages transmitted through communication services;
2.         Section 66B[6] punishes the dishonest receipt of stolen computer resource or communication devices;
3.         Section 66C[7] deals with the protection of personality rights and proscribes identity theft;
4.         Section 66D[8] covers cheating by personation through the medium of a computer resource; and
5.         Section 66E[9] addresses the publishing of private images, in contravention of the Right to Privacy enshrined under Article 21[10], by virtue of Puttaswamy J[11].

A purposive reading of these provisions, rather than adherence to their bare letter, has extended their reach considerably. The provision relating to identity theft has been interpreted to cover the non-consensual use of a person's unique identification features, including but not limited to facial geometry and voice biometrics. This interpretive leap has widened a provision originally drafted for phishing and impersonation, extending it to accommodate the replication of human likeness.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023[12], adds further, covering the ambit of identity theft under Section 319[13], coupled with criminal intimidation and defamation, while the Protection of Women from Cybercrime provisions under the BNS offer certain remedies for sexually explicit deepfakes.

What emerges is not a code but a mirage of code, with borrowed provisions and stretched interpretation, which renders the delivery of justice dependent on two factors: the capability of the lawyer arguing the matter, and the willingness of the honourable Judge to weave the criminal act into the soul of the section.

The IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, notified on 10 February 2026, are India's first legislative effort to curb deepfakes and harmful AI-generated content, introducing "Synthetically Generated Information." Rule 2(1)(wa) defines synthetically generated information as audio, visual or audio-visual information, artificially or algorithmically created, generated, modified or altered using a computer resource, in a manner that such information purports to appear real, authentic or true and depicts or portrays any individual or event in a manner that is, or is likely to be perceived as indistinguishable from a natural person or real-world event.

Significant Social Media Intermediaries are mandated to comply to label AI-generated content with watermark inserted onto the image or video surface. Takedowns of harmful AI-generated or deepfake content within three hours of receiving a complaint or government notification, failing which they risk losing safe harbour protection guaranteed under Section 79 of the IT Act[14].

The 2026 Amendment Rules also condition safe harbour protection under Section 79 on compliance: platforms that knowingly facilitate synthetically generated information in contravention of any statute, or that fail to exercise due diligence by deploying the required detection tools, forfeit that protection.

Lately, a horde of actors including Nandamuri Taraka Rama Rao Jr., R. Madhavan, and Shilpa Shetty secured court orders blocking the dissemination of deepfake videos. This, de facto, indicates that a right to digital personality may be justiciable.

In Sadhguru Jagadish Vasudev & Anr. v. Igor Isakov & Ors., the Delhi High Court introduced and granted an order extending protection against repeated infringement to new mirror and rogue websites, without requiring a suit to be filed. Courts have thus combined personality-rights protection with copyright and trademark doctrine.

Content whose authenticity is questioned must still comply with certification under Section 65B of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. A certificate obtained under Section 65B authenticates that a recording was produced by a functioning device, without taking into account whether the content of that recording is a product of unethical manufacturing or doctoring. It has become common practice in Indian trial courts for evidence to be challenged even after due certification, with defence counsel alleging during cross-examination that a recording is an AI fabrication. In the absence of a statutory threshold, benchmarks, or guidelines for forensic examination, each case must be assessed individually on the reliability of its evidence.

Conclusion
Every legal system eventually meets its limitations, stumbling across a technology that it remains unequipped to handle. Let the facts be clear: four cases were adjudicated in 2024, and nineteen in 2025, numbers disproportional to the incidence of deepfake crimes committed across the country. This reflects an imbalance in the delivery of justice, which leaves the adjudication of deepfake crimes to proceed on a case-by-case, injunction-by-injunction basis. Though the resourcefulness of the Courts — which decline to take the legitimacy of a photograph at face value — must be lauded, improvisation, however skilful it may be, can never be equated to legislative security. Such cases are decided on three factors: the capability of the lawyer to articulate the facts, the unorthodox interpretation of the statute by the Judge, and lastly, perhaps, the privilege of the litigant to possess the resources to litigate it. Ending on an honest note, this makes it one of the more interesting moments to be practising law in the country.

title: Stateless by Design
author: Sanskrati Jain
excerpt: Can a child be denied a nationality because of their parents' immigration status? This article examines the gaps in India's citizenship framework and explores the legal reforms needed to prevent statelessness.
content:
Children must not suffer for their parents’ lack of documentation. Unfortunately, this is the case in India. A child born in India is protected by neither the Citizenship Act, 1955 (“Act”) nor by certain international frameworks such as Convention on the Rights of the Child (“CRC”). This is not merely a consequence of a gap in implementation; rather, it reflects the legal position under Indian law. However, this does not apply to every child born in India. It specifically affects children born to an "illegal migrant," as defined under the Act.

What Does the Law Say?

Since 2003, Section 3(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 demands that a child born in India must be born to parents that are both Indian citizens or one that is an Indian citizen and other that is not an “illegal migrant”.  Additionally, a proviso inserted in Section 2(1)(b) of the Act through an amendment in 2019 categorically excludes children of Muslim migrants from obtaining citizenship.  An “illegal migrant” as defined in Section 2(1)(b) of the Act is a person that has either entered the country without authorised documents such as a valid passport or with valid documents but continues to reside beyond permitted duration.  
In situations where citizenship is in question, it becomes important to consult not only domestic but also international legal standards. Indian law treats citizenship as a right to be inherited and not an immediate entitlement upon birth.  Article 7 of the CRC, on the other hand explicitly accords a child with the right to a nationality immediately upon birth.  The same provision ensures that a child remains protected, stating that parties to the convention must abide by and effectively implement the obligations to the convention particularly when a child may be rendered stateless due to discrepancies in domestic law. India accepted the obligation of the right to a nationality in 1992 but did not ratify a specific enforcement or redressal system for the same. The 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons seeks to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of race, religion or country of origin.  The 1961 Convention on Reduction of Statelessness obligates parties to create protections to prevent statelessness at birth and later in life and providing nationality to children born in countries where they would otherwise be rendered stateless.

The CRC together with the 1954 and 1961 conventions would provide for a seamless protection and redressal system for children born in India that could be rendered stateless due to domestic law. However, India is not a party to either the 1954 Convention or the 1961 Convention. This creates a legal vacuum for children born in such unfortunate circumstances, wherein each legal framework is internally coherent and defensible on its own terms and so, children who fall within this gap are left without effective protection. The issue is that for a child born in India to a parent that is an “illegal migrant” there is no single institution that can be individually held responsible, and this creates a harder battle for the child to defend his or her right to acquire a nationality.

The most practical solution lies within the Act itself. Section 5 already permits citizenship by registration for specific categories of persons, including minor children of Indian citizens,  and this same mechanism could be extended to children who would otherwise be rendered stateless under Section 3(1)(c) . This does not require inventing a new legislative framework, only widening an existing one to a population currently excluded from it. Complete ratification of the 1961 Convention, with its broad obligation to grant nationality in most circumstances, may not be a step India is prepared to take, particularly for a country managing a population of 1.4 billion, but a registration pathway carries none of that structural risk and addresses the same issue at its root. Ratifying the 1954 Convention would remain a useful complementary step, ensuring that children who fall through the cracks are at least treated with dignity and free from discrimination, but it cannot substitute for a domestic mechanism that prevents statelessness at birth in the first place.

Ultimately, this issue extends beyond inconsistencies in the law. It concerns identity, belonging, dignity, and legal security for children. No child should have to go through battles of nationality throughout their childhood and later adulthood, protections must exist and if they fail, clearly established redressal systems must be there to secure the child.
